claims.evidence: Supported by citations to recent research on effort and action selection.

claims.claim: Effort is thought to be minimized whenever possible.
claims.source: Effort is thought to be minimized whenever possible (Hull, 1943; Tsai, 1932), likely because it is costly to spend inherently limited cognitive resources (Friston, 2010; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on effort minimization.

claims.claim: It is costly to spend inherently limited cognitive resources.
claims.source: Effort is thought to be minimized whenever possible (Hull, 1943; Tsai, 1932), likely because it is costly to spend inherently limited cognitive resources (Friston, 2010; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on cognitive resources.

claims.claim: Saccades are relatively affordable (not very costly).
claims.source: Although saccades are relatively affordable [i.e. not very costly; Findlay and Gilchrist, 2003; Theeuwes, 2012], they are executed very often (Henderson, 2003; Henderson and Hollingworth, 1998) and, therefore, even small costs should add up over time (Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020; Koevoet et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade costs.

claims.claim: Even small saccade costs should add up over time because saccades are executed very often.
claims.source: Although saccades are relatively affordable [i.e. not very costly; Findlay and Gilchrist, 2003; Theeuwes, 2012], they are executed very often (Henderson, 2003; Henderson and Hollingworth, 1998) and, therefore, even small costs should add up over time (Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020; Koevoet et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on saccade frequency and cost accumulation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Computational models suggest that saccade costs predict saccade behavior.
claims.source: This would be in line with recent evidence from computational models suggesting that saccade costs predict saccade behavior [e.g. Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2019; Kadner et al., 2022; Thomas et al., 2022].
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claims.claim: Previous studies either assumed saccade costs or indirectly inferred them from gaze behavior itself.
claims.source: These studies either assumed saccade costs or indirectly inferred them from gaze behavior itself.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of prior research methods in the field.

claims.claim: No study has been able to quantify saccade costs (neuro-)physiologically until recently.
claims.source: However, no study has been able to quantify saccade costs (neuro-)physiologically, and therefore been able to directly test this hypothesis until recently.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the field prior to recent work.

claims.claim: The effort of saccade planning can be measured with pupil size when low-level visual factors are controlled for.
claims.source: We recently demonstrated that the effort of saccade planning can be measured with pupil size, which allows for a physiological quantification of saccade costs as long as low-level visual factors are controlled for (Koevoet et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, cited here.

claims.claim: Loading more in working memory results in stronger pupil dilation.
claims.source: For instance, loading more in working memory or tracking more objects results in stronger pupil dilation (Beatty, 1982; Koevoet et al., 2024; Robison and Unsworth, 2019; Alnæs et al., 2014; Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Unsworth and Miller, 2021; Unsworth and Robison, 2015; Ahern and Beatty, 1979; Hess and Polt, 1964).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on pupil dilation and working memory.

claims.claim: Tracking more objects results in stronger pupil dilation.
claims.source: For instance, loading more in working memory or tracking more objects results in stronger pupil dilation (Beatty, 1982; Koevoet et al., 2024; Robison and Unsworth, 2019; Alnæs et al., 2014; Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Unsworth and Miller, 2021; Unsworth and Robison, 2015; Ahern and Beatty, 1979; Hess and Polt, 1964).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on pupil dilation and object tracking.

claims.claim: Pupil size reflects not only cognitive effort but also the effort of planning and executing movements.
claims.source: Pupil size not only reflects cognitive (or mental) effort but also the effort of planning and executing movements (Naber and Murphy, 2020; Richer and Beatty, 1985; Bumke, 1911).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on pupil size and movement effort.

claims.claim: Saccade costs are higher for oblique compared with cardinal directions.
claims.source: We leveraged this to demonstrate that saccade costs can be captured with pupil size, and are higher for oblique compared with cardinal directions (Koevoet et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, cited here.

claims.claim: Pupil size differed across saccade directions during saccade planning.
claims.source: Replicating our previous findings, we found that pupil size differed across directions (Koevoet et al., 2023; Figure 1c–f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study, shown in Figure 1c-f.

claims.claim: Pupil size during planning of oblique saccades was larger compared with cardinal saccades.
claims.source: We observed a larger pupil size during planning of oblique saccades compared with cardinal saccades (β = 7.662, SE  = 1.957, t = 3.916, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study's data analysis.

claims.claim: Downward saccades were associated with a larger pupil size than upward saccades.
claims.source: Downward saccades were associated with a larger pupil size than upward saccades (β = 0.556, SE  = 0.171, t = 3.261, p = 0.001)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study's data analysis.

claims.claim: Pupil size was slightly larger for leftward compared with rightward saccades.
claims.source: and we found a slightly larger pupil size for leftward compared with rightward saccades (β = 0.226, SE  = 0.095, t = 2.388, p = 0.017).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study's data analysis.

claims.claim: The effects of saccade direction on pupil size were not mediated by differences in saccade properties such as duration, amplitude, peak velocity, and landing precision.
claims.source: These effects were not mediated by differences in saccade properties, such as duration, amplitude, peak velocity, and landing precision (Figure 1e and f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study's statistical analysis, shown in Figure 1e and f.

claims.claim: Saccade costs differ as a function of direction.
claims.source: Together, this shows that saccade costs differ as a function of direction, indicating that certain saccades are more costly than others.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pupil size data across directions.

claims.claim: Participants preferred cardinal over oblique saccade directions.
claims.source: Results showed that participants preferred cardinal over oblique directions (β = 0.091, SE = 0.023, t = 3.910, p < 0.001; Figure 2b)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade preference task, shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Participants preferred upward over downward saccade directions.
claims.source: and preferred upward over downward directions (β = 0.036, SE = 0.017, t = 2.130, p = 0.033).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade preference task.

claims.claim: No differences were observed between leftward and rightward saccade directions in preferences.
claims.source: No differences were observed between leftward and rightward saccade directions (β = 0.009, SE = 0.014, t = 0.668, p = 0.504).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade preference task.

claims.claim: Pupil size during saccade planning negatively correlated with saccade preferences.
claims.source: In line with our hypothesis, pupil size during saccade planning (in cued directions) negatively correlated with saccade preferences (during self-selection) (r(34) = –0.76, p < 0.001; Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlating the two tasks, shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: Intrinsic saccade costs critically predict saccade preferences.
claims.source: For the first time, this demonstrates that intrinsic saccade costs critically predict saccade preferences.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between pupil size and preferences.

claims.claim: Participants preferred saccading towards affordable over costly options.
claims.source: Put differently, participants preferred saccading towards affordable over costly options.
claims.evidence: This is a restatement of the main finding from the preference task.

claims.claim: The correlation between pupil size and saccade preferences was not driven by other oculomotor metrics such as saccade latency and landing precision.
claims.source: A control analysis ruled out that the correlation between pupil size and saccade preferences was driven by other oculomotor metrics such as saccade latency and landing precision (see Supporting Information).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Pupil sizes during saccade planning were smaller for preferred directions than for avoided directions.
claims.source: Illustrating the robustness of this relationship further, we found smaller pupil sizes during saccade planning for preferred (selected >50%) than for avoided (selected <50%) directions (t(19) = 4.38, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.979; Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing preferred vs avoided directions, shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: Saccade costs predicted saccade selection on a trial-by-trial basis.
claims.source: As another test of the robustness of the effect, we analyzed whether saccade costs predicted saccade selection on a trial-by-trial basis.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a trial-by-trial analysis in the study.

claims.claim: The more affordable option was chosen above chance level (56.64%) across participants.
claims.source: Complementing the above analyses, the more affordable option was chosen above chance level across participants (M = 56.64%, 95% CI = [52.75–60.52%], one-sample t-test against 50%: t(19) = 3.26, p = 0.004, Cohen's d = 0.729; Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the trial-by-trial analysis, shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: Saccade costs robustly predict saccade preferences.
claims.source: Together, these analyses established that saccade costs robustly predict saccade preferences.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple converging analyses.

claims.claim: Saccade curvature reflects conflict between target and distractor saccade vectors.
claims.source: Saccade curvature reflects conflict between target and distractor saccade vectors: if a distractor is inhibited, and the target is activated, the saccade curves away from the distractor location (Van der Stigchel et al., 2006; McPeek et al., 2003; Van der Stigchel, 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade curvature.

claims.claim: When saccade costs differ more between directions, there should be more conflict between saccade vectors.
claims.source: Whenever saccade costs differ more between directions, there should, therefore, be more conflict between saccade vectors.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the relationship between cost differences and conflict.

claims.claim: If both saccade directions were equally costly, there would be no need for conflict as cost minimization is impossible.
claims.source: If both directions were equally costly, there would be no need for conflict as cost minimization is impossible.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between cost differences and conflict.

claims.claim: Weighing costs and reward in decision-making takes time.
claims.source: Furthermore, weighing costs (and reward) in decision-making is known to take time (Spering, 2022, Polanía et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on decision-making time.

claims.claim: More elaborate decisions should show in more curvature and longer saccade latencies.
claims.source: More elaborate decisions should, therefore, not only show in more curvature, but also in longer saccade latencies.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from the relationship between decision complexity and oculomotor properties.

claims.claim: Saccades curved away from the non-selected option in the majority of trials (78.15%).
claims.source: Saccades curved away from the non-selected option in the majority of trials, indicating oculomotor conflict (Figure 3a; M = 78.15%, 95% CI = [74.734–81.567%], t(19) = 15.741, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 3.519).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade curvature analysis, shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: When the difference in pupil size between two saccade options was larger, saccades curved away more from the non-selected option.
claims.source: Whenever the difference in pupil size between the two options was larger, saccades curved away more from the non-selected option (β = 0.004, SE  = 0.001, t = 4.448, p < 0.001; Figure 3b)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of curvature and cost differences, shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: When the difference in pupil size between two saccade options was larger, saccade latencies slowed.
claims.source: and their latencies slowed (β = 0.050, SE  = 0.013, t = 4.323, p < 0.001; Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of latency and cost differences, shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Cost is actively weighed during saccade selection and leads to stronger conflict when cost differences are larger.
claims.source: Our results show that cost is actively weighed and leads to stronger conflict whenever cost differences are larger.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the curvature and latency findings.

claims.claim: More elaborate decisions in saccade selection are predominantly made when warranted by sufficient differences in saccade costs between options.
claims.source: This suggests that more elaborate decisions in saccade selection are predominantly made when warranted by sufficient differences in saccade costs between options.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between cost differences and decision complexity.

claims.claim: Pupil size predicted saccade selection above chance (59.72%) when saccades curved away from the non-selected option.
claims.source: Pupil size (i.e. saccade cost) predicted saccade selection when saccades curved away (M = 59.72%, 95% CI = [55.208–64.233%], t(19) = 4.116, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.920)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the trial-by-trial analysis split by curvature direction.

claims.claim: Pupil size did not predict saccade selection when saccades curved toward the non-selected option.
claims.source: but not toward (M = 48.42%, 95% CI = [44.496–52.338%], t(19) = 0.771, P = 0.450, Cohen's d = 0.172) the non-selected option.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the trial-by-trial analysis split by curvature direction.

claims.claim: Prediction accuracies differed between toward and away curving saccades.
claims.source: These prediction accuracies differed between curve directions (t(19) = 4.795, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.072; Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing prediction accuracies, shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: Saccade costs were predominantly considered when saccades curved away from the non-selected option.
claims.source: This shows that saccade costs were predominantly considered when saccades curved away.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential prediction accuracies.

claims.claim: The costs of potential saccade targets are especially weighed during saccade selection when warranted by large differences in saccade costs.
claims.source: Together, these analyses suggest that the costs of potential saccade targets are especially weighed during saccade selection when warranted by large differences in saccade costs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the curvature and prediction accuracy analyses.

claims.claim: When cost differences are large, oculomotor conflict increases and saccade cost plays a bigger role in saccade selection.
claims.source: In these cases, oculomotor conflict increases and saccade cost plays a bigger role in saccade selection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the relationship between cost differences, conflict, and selection.

claims.claim: A negative relationship was observed between pupil size and saccade preferences in Experiment 1 of natural viewing.
claims.source: As hypothesized, we observed a negative relationship between pupil size and saccade preferences in both experiments (Exp. 1: β = 1.784, SE  = 0.324, t = 5.412, p < 0.001; saccade preferences in Figure 4b, link in Figure 4c
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the natural viewing data analysis, shown in Figures 4b and 4c.

claims.claim: A negative relationship was observed between pupil size and saccade preferences in Experiment 2 of natural viewing.
claims.source: Exp. 2: β = 0.644, SE  = 0.170, t = 3.780, p < 0.001; saccade preferences in Figure 4d, link in Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the natural viewing data analysis, shown in Figures 4d and 4e.

claims.claim: Even when participants made unconstrained eye movements in natural scenes, saccade cost remained linked to saccade preferences.
claims.source: This shows that even when participants made unconstrained eye movements in natural scenes, saccade cost remained linked to saccade preferences: affordable directions were preferred over costly directions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the natural viewing experiments.

claims.claim: The additional cognitive demand of the dual task led to a decreased saccade frequency.
claims.source: The additional cognitive demand of the dual task indeed led to a decreased saccade frequency (t(24) = 7.224, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.445; Figure 4h).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the dual-task manipulation, shown in Figure 4h.

claims.claim: The auditory dual task and the oculomotor system, at least in part, consumed from a shared pool of cognitive resources.
claims.source: This indicates that the auditory dual task and the oculomotor system, at least in part, consumed from a shared pool of cognitive resources.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the decreased saccade frequency under dual-task conditions.

claims.claim: Pupil size negatively linked with the saccade adjustment map between single and dual tasks.
claims.source: Nevertheless, pupil size negatively linked with the adjustment map as hypothesized (β = 9.333, SE  = 0.966, t = 9.659, p < 0.001; Figure 4i; while controlling for the same possible covariates as before).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the adjustment analysis, shown in Figure 4i.

claims.claim: Costly saccades were cut disproportionally when more cognitive resources were consumed by the additional auditory dual task.
claims.source: This shows that costly saccades were cut disproportionally when more cognitive resources were consumed by the additional auditory dual task.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the negative relationship between pupil size and adjustment.

claims.claim: Cognitive resources are flexibly (dis)allocated from and to the oculomotor system based on the current resource demands.
claims.source: This demonstrates that cognitive resources are flexibly (dis)allocated from and to the oculomotor system based on the current resource demands.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dual-task findings.

claims.claim: Affordable saccades were preferred over costly ones.
claims.source: We observed that affordable saccades were preferred over costly ones.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the preference task.

claims.claim: When two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, higher oculomotor conflict was found as indexed by stronger saccade trajectory deviations away from the non-selected option.
claims.source: Furthermore, when two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, we found higher oculomotor conflict as indexed by stronger saccade trajectory deviations away from the non-selected option and increased onset latencies.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the curvature and latency analyses.

claims.claim: When two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, increased onset latencies were found.
claims.source: Furthermore, when two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, we found higher oculomotor conflict as indexed by stronger saccade trajectory deviations away from the non-selected option and increased onset latencies.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the curvature and latency analyses.

claims.claim: Saccade directions were flexibly adjusted based on cost as cognitive demand increased.
claims.source: Lastly, saccade directions were flexibly adjusted based on cost as cognitive demand increased.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the dual-task experiment.

claims.claim: Saccade costs fundamentally underlie saccade selection, even when physical salience, the goals of the observer, and selection history affect where the eyes are moved.
claims.source: Together, this demonstrates that saccade costs fundamentally underlie saccade selection, even when physical salience, the goals of the observer, and selection history affect where the eyes are moved.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experiments in the study.

claims.claim: At least three processes contribute to the total cost of a saccade: the complexity of oculomotor programming, shifting of presaccadic attention, and predictive/spatial remapping.
claims.source: We speculate that at least three processes contribute to the total cost of a saccade (Koevoet et al., 2023): the complexity of oculomotor programming (Jainta et al., 2011; Wang and Munoz, 2021; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020), shifting of presaccadic attention (Rizzolatti et al., 1987; Deubel and Schneider, 1996), and predictive/spatial remapping (Rolfs, 2015; Melcher, 2007; Bays and Husain, 2007; Fabius et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior research, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Oblique but not cardinal saccades require communication between pontine and midbrain circuits.
claims.source: For example, oblique but not cardinal saccades require communication between pontine and midbrain circuits (Sparks, 2002; King and Fuchs, 1979; Curthoys et al., 1984).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade neural circuitry.

claims.claim: Differences in neural complexity may underlie the additional costs of oblique compared with cardinal saccades.
claims.source: Such differences in neural complexity may underlie the additional costs of oblique compared with cardinal saccades.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference about the neural basis of saccade costs.

claims.claim: Presaccadic attention is shifted prior to each saccade to prepare the brain for the abrupt changes in retinal input resulting from saccades through spatial/predictive remapping.
claims.source: Furthermore, presaccadic attention is shifted prior to each saccade to prepare the brain for the abrupt changes in retinal input resulting from saccades through spatial/predictive remapping (Melcher and Colby, 2008; Rolfs, 2015; Melcher, 2007; Bays and Husain, 2007; Rizzolatti et al., 1987; Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Van der Stigchel and Hollingworth, 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on presaccadic attention and remapping.

claims.claim: Preparation for upcoming changes in retinal input consumes neurocognitive resources and likely contributes to saccade costs.
claims.source: This preparation for upcoming changes in retinal input consumes neurocognitive resources and, therefore, likely also contributes to saccade costs (Koevoet et al., 2023; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in perception.
claims.source: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in perception (Wexler et al., 2022; Barbot et al., 2021; Baldwin et al., 2012; Greenwood et al., 2017; Chakravarthi et al., 2022; Abrams et al., 2012; Ezzo et al., 2023)
claims.evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in attention.
claims.source: attention (Hanning et al., 2024; Hanning et al., 2022; Schütz, 2014; Carrasco et al., 2001; Mackeben, 1999; Ohl et al., 2024)
claims.evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in saccade characteristics.
claims.source: saccade characteristics (Hanning et al., 2024; Greenwood et al., 2017; Hanning et al., 2022; Ohl et al., 2024)
claims.evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in (early) visual cortex.
claims.source: and (early) visual cortex (Himmelberg et al., 2022; Van Essen et al., 1984; Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2018; also see Himmelberg et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The upper visual field is relatively underrepresented in early visual areas.
claims.source: For example, downward saccades are more costly than upward saccades, which mimics a similar asymmetry in early visual areas wherein the upper visual field is relatively underrepresented (Himmelberg et al., 2022; Van Essen et al., 1984; Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2018)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on visual field representation.

claims.claim: Stronger presaccadic benefits are found for down- compared with upward saccades.
claims.source: similarly stronger presaccadic benefits are found for down- compared with upward saccades (Hanning et al., 2024, Hanning et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on presaccadic attention.

claims.claim: Upward saccades are more precise than downward saccades.
claims.source: Moreover, upward saccades are more precise than downward saccades (Greenwood et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on saccade precision.

claims.claim: Saccade latency has been proposed to index oculomotor effort.
claims.source: For example, saccade latency has been proposed to index oculomotor effort (Shadmehr et al., 2019), whereby saccades with longer latencies are associated with more oculomotor effort.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on saccade latency and effort.

claims.claim: Saccade latency is a possible complementary marker of saccade costs.
claims.source: This makes saccade latency a possible complementary marker of saccade costs (also see Appendix).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about alternative measures of saccade cost.

claims.claim: Pupil size allows capturing not only the costs of saccades, but also of covert attentional shifts.
claims.source: Pupil size, therefore, allows to capture not only the costs of saccades, but also of covert attentional shifts (Koevoet et al., 2023), or shifts with other effectors such as head or arm movements (Richer and Beatty, 1985; Voudouris et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on pupil size and various types of movements.

claims.claim: Pupil size can measure saccade costs even when searching in natural scenes.
claims.source: Second, as we have demonstrated, pupil size can measure saccade costs even when searching in natural scenes (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the natural viewing experiments, shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: During natural viewing, it is difficult to disentangle fixation duration from saccade latencies.
claims.source: During natural viewing, it is difficult to disentangle fixation duration from saccade latencies, complicating the use of saccade latency as a measure of saccade cost.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological observation about measuring saccade latency in natural viewing.

claims.claim: The findings are in line with established effort-based models that assume costs to be weighed against rewards during decision-making.
claims.source: Our findings are in line with established effort-based models that assume costs to be weighed against rewards during decision-making (Kool et al., 2010; Kurzban et al., 2013; Shenhav et al., 2021; Shenhav et al., 2013; Shenhav et al., 2017; Westbrook and Braver, 2015).
claims.evidence: This connects the current findings to prior theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The intrinsic costs of arm movements are considered during decision-making: biomechanically affordable movements are generally preferred over more costly ones.
claims.source: Relatedly, the intrinsic costs of arm movements are also considered during decision-making: biomechanically affordable movements are generally preferred over more costly ones (Cos et al., 2011; Cos et al., 2014; Cos et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on arm movement costs.

claims.claim: Until now, the intrinsic costs of saccades and other movements have been inferred from gaze behavior itself or by using computational modeling.
claims.source: First, until now, the intrinsic costs of saccades and other movements have been inferred from gaze behavior itself or by using computational modeling (Thomas et al., 2022; Kadner et al., 2022; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2019; Cos et al., 2011; Cos et al., 2014; Cos et al., 2012; Petitet et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of prior research methods, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The current study directly measured cost physiologically using pupil size.
claims.source: In contrast, we directly measured cost physiologically using pupil size.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological contribution of the current study.

claims.claim: Physiologically measured saccade costs predict where saccades are directed in a controlled binary preference task and during natural viewing.
claims.source: Second, we show that physiologically measured saccade costs predict where saccades are directed in a controlled binary preference task, and even during natural viewing.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from both the preference task and natural viewing experiments.

claims.claim: Cost-based decision-making may be a general property of the brain.
claims.source: However, cost-based decision-making may be a more general property of the brain (Friston, 2010; Kahneman, 1973; Attneave, 1959; Hasenstaub et al., 2010; Jamadar et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the generality of cost-based decision-making, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Every action, be it physical or cognitive, is associated with an intrinsic cost.
claims.source: Every action, be it physical or cognitive, is associated with an intrinsic cost, and pupil size is likely a general marker of this (Beatty, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the generality of action costs, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Pupil dilation does not always reflect cost, as the pupil dilates in response to many sensory and cognitive factors.
claims.source: Note, however, that pupil dilation does not always reflect cost, as the pupil dilates in response to many sensory and cognitive factors which should be controlled for, or at least considered, when interpreting pupillometric data [e.g., see Mathôt and Vilotijević, 2023; Strauch et al., 2022; Mathôt, 2018; Sirois and Brisson, 2014].
claims.evidence: This is a methodological caveat about interpreting pupil size, supported by citations.

results.result: Pupil size during saccade planning differs systematically across saccade directions, with oblique saccades showing larger pupil sizes than cardinal saccades, downward saccades larger than upward, and leftward slightly larger than rightward. These effects are not mediated by differences in saccade properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 present converging statistical evidence from linear mixed-effects models showing directional differences in pupil size during saccade planning (p<0.001 for oblique vs cardinal, p=0.001 for vertical, p=0.017 for horizontal). Control analyses (C33) rule out confounding by saccade properties. The findings replicate prior work (C29) and are visualized in Figure 1c-f.

results.result: Saccade costs, as measured by pupil size during planning, robustly predict saccade preferences in a free-choice task. Participants preferred cardinal over oblique directions and upward over downward directions, with a strong negative correlation (r=-0.76, p<0.001) between pupil size and preference. The more affordable option was chosen above chance (56.64%) on a trial-by-trial basis.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C45 provide multiple converging lines of evidence: directional preferences mirror cost patterns (C35-C37), strong correlation between pupil size and preferences (C38, p<0.001), preferred directions show smaller pupil sizes (C42, Cohen's d=0.979), and above-chance trial-by-trial prediction (C44, p=0.004). Control analyses rule out confounds (C41). This represents the first physiological demonstration linking saccade costs to preferences.

results.result: Larger differences in saccade costs between two options lead to increased oculomotor conflict, as evidenced by greater saccade curvature away from the non-selected option and longer saccade latencies. Saccade costs predict selection above chance (59.72%) specifically when saccades curve away from the non-selected option, but not when curving toward it.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C61 demonstrate that cost differences modulate decision-making signatures: larger pupil size differences predict more curvature (C52, p<0.001) and longer latencies (C53, p<0.001). The differential prediction accuracy between away-curving (59.72%, p<0.001) and toward-curving saccades (48.42%, p=0.450) provides strong evidence that costs are actively weighed during conflict resolution (C56-C59). Statistical tests confirm differences between conditions (C58, p<0.001).

results.result: The negative relationship between pupil size and saccade preferences generalizes to natural scene viewing in two independent experiments, with participants preferring affordable over costly saccade directions even during unconstrained eye movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 extend the main finding to ecologically valid conditions. Both natural viewing experiments show significant negative relationships between pupil size and preferences (Exp 1: β=1.784, p<0.001; Exp 2: β=0.644, p<0.001), despite the complexity of natural scenes and the need to control for multiple confounding factors. This demonstrates the robustness and generalizability of the cost-preference relationship.

results.result: Under increased cognitive demand from an auditory dual task, participants made fewer saccades overall and disproportionately cut costly saccade directions. This demonstrates that cognitive resources are flexibly allocated between the oculomotor system and other cognitive operations based on current demands.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C65-C69 provide causal evidence through experimental manipulation. The dual task significantly reduced saccade frequency (C65, Cohen's d=1.445, p<0.001), and pupil size negatively predicted which directions were cut (C67, p<0.001), with costly saccades disproportionately avoided (C68). This supports the resource-sharing hypothesis (C66, C69) and demonstrates adaptive resource allocation (C108).

results.result: Pupil size is an established marker of effort that can measure saccade costs when low-level visual factors are controlled, with prior work demonstrating higher costs for oblique compared to cardinal saccades.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C24-C28 establish the methodological foundation through extensive citations to prior work. C1 is supported by 9 citations establishing pupil size as an effort marker. C24 and C28 cite the authors' previous work validating this approach for saccades. C25-C27 provide additional supporting evidence from the broader pupillometry literature. This represents well-established prior knowledge.

results.result: The main conclusion that effort drives saccade selection, with participants consistently preferring less costly saccade directions across multiple experimental contexts, including natural scene viewing.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C70-C74 represent the overarching conclusions drawn from all experimental findings. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from the preference task (C3), natural viewing experiments (C4), dual-task manipulation (C5-C6), and oculomotor conflict analyses (C51-C61). The conclusion integrates effort with established factors in saccade selection (C124).

results.result: Theoretical predictions about how cost differences should affect oculomotor conflict: larger cost differences should produce more conflict (curvature) and longer decision times (latencies).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 establish the theoretical framework linking cost differences to oculomotor signatures. C46 is supported by citations to established work on saccade curvature. C47-C48 present logical inferences about the relationship between cost differences and conflict. C49 is supported by citations on decision-making time. These predictions are subsequently confirmed by the empirical findings in C51-C61.

results.result: Speculation about the neural and cognitive processes that contribute to saccade costs, including oculomotor programming complexity, presaccadic attention shifts, and spatial remapping, as well as potential links to perceptual and cortical anisotropies.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C83 are explicitly speculative (C75 states 'we speculate') and represent hypotheses about underlying mechanisms rather than tested findings. While supported by citations to relevant literature, these claims go beyond what the current data can demonstrate. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation, noting that 'future work should elucidate which processes contribute to saccade costs' and that their data 'do not allow direct inferences' about neural mechanisms.

results.result: Discussion of pupil size as a measure of saccade costs, including its advantages (generality, applicability to natural viewing) and complementary measures (saccade latency).
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 discuss methodological considerations. C87 is supported by citation. C88 is appropriately framed as speculative. C89 is supported by citations. C90 is demonstrated by the natural viewing experiments (Figure 4). C91 presents a valid methodological observation. These claims appropriately characterize the strengths and limitations of the pupillometric approach.

results.result: The current study advances the field by directly measuring saccade costs physiologically using pupil size, in contrast to prior work that inferred costs from behavior or computational models. This physiological measure predicts saccade selection in both controlled and natural viewing contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 position the work relative to prior research. C92-C94 accurately characterize prior approaches through citations. C95 correctly identifies the methodological contribution. C96 summarizes the empirical findings. This represents a fair assessment of the study's novelty and contribution to the literature.

results.result: Broader theoretical discussion of cost-based decision-making as a general brain principle, the neural basis of effort-linked pupil dilation (locus coeruleus), and potential metabolic markers of cost.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C104 present broader theoretical context. C97-C98 are appropriately framed as speculative. C99 provides an important methodological caveat supported by citations. C100-C103 discuss the neural basis with appropriate citations. C104 is explicitly tentative ('tentative evidence even suggests'). While these claims are well-grounded in the literature, they extend beyond what the current study directly demonstrates and are appropriately presented as context and speculation.

results.result: Theoretical framework proposing that limited cognitive resources must be distributed between the oculomotor system and other cognitive operations, with evidence from prior work showing altered eye movements under cognitive load.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C115 develop the theoretical framework for resource allocation. C105 is established knowledge. C106-C107 are logical inferences supported by citations. C109-C114 cite prior empirical work demonstrating resource competition. C115 represents the theoretical proposal supported by the dual-task findings (C65-C69). This framework is well-grounded in prior literature and supported by the current experimental evidence.

results.result: Discussion of the neural circuitry potentially underlying saccade cost computation and selection, including the oculomotor-decision making network.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 discuss neural mechanisms. C116-C117 accurately characterize established knowledge about oculomotor and decision-making networks through extensive citations. However, C118 is appropriately framed as speculative ('it is plausible'). The authors correctly note that their 'data do not allow direct inferences about the precise neural circuitry.' These claims represent informed speculation rather than tested hypotheses.

results.result: Argument that only a cost account can explain the full pattern of findings: the link between pupil size and preferences, cardinal bias, reduced saccade frequency under cognitive load, and selective cutting of costly directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 present a logical argument for the cost account based on the convergent evidence. Each prediction (C119-C122) is supported by specific empirical findings in the study. This represents a valid inference from the data, though alternative explanations are not explicitly tested. The argument is strengthened by the multiple converging lines of evidence across different experimental manipulations.

results.result: Background establishing the frequency of saccades, known factors driving saccade selection (bottom-up, top-down, selection history), systematic biases in eye movements, and the theoretical importance of effort in action selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C23 establish the background and motivation for the study. All are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (C9, C11-C14, C16-C23) or represent logical inferences from established knowledge (C10, C15, C20). These claims accurately characterize the state of the field and identify the gap that the current study addresses (C22-C23).

results.result: Statement that saccade costs predicted saccade selection on a trial-by-trial basis.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is directly supported by the statistical finding in C44, which shows above-chance prediction (56.64%, p=0.004). This represents a valid summary of the trial-by-trial analysis results.

results.result: Inference that the eye-movement system and other cognitive operations consume similar resources that are flexibly allocated based on cognitive demand.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is an inference drawn from the dual-task findings (C5-C6, C65-C69). The experimental evidence showing reduced saccade frequency and selective cutting of costly directions under cognitive load provides strong support for this resource-sharing hypothesis. This represents a valid inference from the causal manipulation.

results.result: Examples of established anisotropies in visual processing and saccade characteristics that parallel the observed cost differences (e.g., upper visual field underrepresentation, presaccadic attention asymmetries, saccade precision differences).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 cite specific prior findings that parallel the observed cost patterns. Each is supported by appropriate citations. These represent accurate characterizations of prior work that provide potential mechanistic context for the observed cost differences, though the causal relationships remain to be established.

results.result: The authors claim that pupil size is a well-established and physiologically valid marker of effort, including saccade-related effort (saccade costs), with pupil dilation linked to locus coeruleus activity and neural resource expenditure.
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly challenges the interpretation that pupil size indexes effort/cost, stating 'what is at issue is the interpretation' and that 'how the conclusion follows from the propositions is not self-evident.' The reviewer notes that the authors 'do not consider plausible alternatives' and criticizes the theoretical framework as 'too impoverished,' pointing out missing consideration of cholinergic and dopamine systems. The reviewer also raises incompatible observations about pupil size in speed-accuracy tradeoffs that the authors do not address.

results.result: Pupil size during saccade planning differed systematically across saccade directions, with oblique saccades showing larger pupil sizes than cardinal saccades, downward larger than upward, and leftward slightly larger than rightward. These effects were not mediated by differences in saccade properties.
results.evaluation: The reviewer states 'a relationship between pupil size and saccade production seems clear based on the authors' previous and current work' and notes the 'clarity of the findings.' The editor also describes 'relatively clear and convincing results of the relationship between pupil size and saccade production.' These directional differences in pupil size are accepted as empirical findings.

results.result: In a binary choice task, participants consistently preferred less costly (affordable) saccade directions over more costly ones, with pupil size during saccade planning negatively correlating with saccade preferences. Cardinal directions were preferred over oblique, upward over downward, and the more affordable option was chosen above chance (56.64%).
results.evaluation: While the empirical relationship between pupil size and saccade preferences is acknowledged as clear, the reviewer questions the interpretation that this reflects 'cost' minimization. The reviewer states 'what is at issue is the interpretation' and asks 'Is "cost" the only conceivable hypothesis?' The reviewer also notes that 'the authors draw conclusions based on trends across participants, but they should be more transparent about variation that contradicts these trends,' pointing to participants in Figures 3 and 4 who 'look so different.'

results.result: When cost differences between saccade options were larger (measured by pupil size differences), saccades showed greater curvature away from the non-selected option and longer latencies, indicating increased oculomotor conflict. Pupil size predicted saccade selection above chance only when saccades curved away from the non-selected option.
results.evaluation: The reviewer acknowledges the 'clarity of the findings' regarding the relationship between pupil size differences and oculomotor measures (curvature, latency). However, the interpretation that this reflects 'cost' weighing is questioned given the broader critique of the cost framework. The reviewer also raises concerns about individual differences, noting participants who 'look so different' in the figures, questioning whether this is 'just noise, or do different participants adopt different policies?'

results.result: The principle that affordable saccade directions are preferred over costly ones held even during unconstrained search in natural scenes across two experiments, with pupil size negatively correlating with saccade preferences in both experiments.
results.evaluation: While the empirical finding of the relationship between pupil size and saccade preferences in natural scenes is part of the 'clear and convincing results' noted by reviewers, the interpretation as cost-based selection remains questioned. The reviewer's fundamental challenge to the cost interpretation framework applies equally to these natural scene experiments, as they rely on the same pupil-size-as-cost premise that the reviewer finds insufficiently justified.

results.result: Under increased cognitive demand from a dual auditory counting task, participants made fewer saccades overall and disproportionately cut costly saccade directions, suggesting that the oculomotor system and cognitive operations share resources that are flexibly allocated based on demand.
results.evaluation: The empirical finding of reduced saccade frequency under dual-task conditions is likely accepted, but the interpretation that this reflects shared resource allocation and cost-based adjustment is subject to the reviewer's broader critique of the cost framework. The reviewer's concern about alternative hypotheses and the theoretical framework being 'too impoverished' applies to this interpretation of resource sharing and flexible allocation.

results.result: The authors speculate that at least three processes contribute to saccade costs: complexity of oculomotor programming (with oblique saccades requiring communication between pontine and midbrain circuits), shifting of presaccadic attention, and predictive/spatial remapping.
results.evaluation: The reviewer directly challenges the mechanistic explanation, stating: 'the basis of the claim that more neurons in FEF and SC are needed for oblique versus cardinal saccades is not established in any of the publications cited' and 'the authors may be referring to the fact that oblique saccades require coordination between pontine and midbrain circuits. This must be clarified.' The reviewer also questions the source and currency of cost, asking 'if net muscle contraction is the cost, then why are upward saccades, which require the eyelid, not more expensive than downward? Thus, just how some saccades are more effortful than others is not clear.'

results.result: The authors conclude that eye-movement behavior is tuned to adaptively minimize saccade-inherent effort, and that saccade costs fundamentally underlie saccade selection alongside physical salience, observer goals, and selection history. They propose that effort is a fundamental factor driving saccade selection.
results.evaluation: The reviewer fundamentally questions this conclusion, stating that the authors 'test one, preferred hypothesis and do not consider plausible alternatives' and that 'the logical structure of this manuscript can be criticized as committing the fallacy of affirming the consequent.' The reviewer notes that 'the theoretical perspective of this manuscript as too impoverished' and suggests the work 'may be enhanced by consideration of other work on this general topic.' While the editor notes the findings are 'important,' the reviewer's concerns about interpretation and alternative hypotheses leave the main theoretical conclusion uncertain.

OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, peer reviewer also rates as SUPPORTED, noting 'clarity of the findings' and that 'a relationship between pupil size and saccade production seems clear.'

Strong disagreement on interpretation (C1, C2, C24, C27, C28, C100, C103). OpenEval rates the methodological foundation as SUPPORTED based on established literature. Peer reviewer rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly challenging 'what is at issue is the interpretation' of pupil size as effort/cost marker, stating the theoretical framework is 'too impoverished' and criticizing lack of consideration of cholinergic and dopamine systems.

Also raises concerns about individual variation contradicting group trends.
